advances: Supplies the reusable exact finite reduction for common-vertex homothetic triangles. For every fixed middle-slice point, it replaces the continuum of directions and slopes by finitely many rational or real-algebraic polynomial systems. It does not close the specialized fixed-triple subgoal.
author: mp_r9_normal_form
proof:
An affine planar map taking the common vertex and the other two vertices to \(0,e_1,e_2\) maps halfspaces bijectively to halfspaces and multiplies all slice areas by the same positive determinant. It therefore suffices to use the stated normalization and retain the common factor \(D\).

By accepted lemma `400272f6de6c67bb`, the depth at \((1,z)\) may be computed from boundary-through-\((1,z)\) halfspaces, together with the two horizontal halfspaces. Every nonhorizontal such halfspace has form (1). Since \(L\ne0\), its values on a nondegenerate triangle are not all equal, so positive rescaling gives (2). Ordering the values gives a permutation \(\pi\) and \(\rho=c_{\pi_1}-c_{\pi_0}\in[0,1]\). Because \(c_0=0\), the location of vertex \(0\) in the ordering forces precisely the three cases in (4). This proves the direction parametrization, including all six oriented chambers and their tied boundaries.

For \(0<\rho<1\), a threshold between the two lower projected vertex values cuts off a triangle similar to the minimum-vertex corner. Its area ratio is
\[
\frac{(t-\gamma)^2}
{(c_{\pi_1}-c_{\pi_0})(c_{\pi_2}-c_{\pi_0})}
=
\frac{(t-\gamma)^2}{\rho}.
\]
Above the middle value, the omitted maximum-vertex corner has area ratio
\[
\frac{(\gamma+1-t)^2}
{(c_{\pi_2}-c_{\pi_0})(c_{\pi_2}-c_{\pi_1})}
=
\frac{(\gamma+1-t)^2}{1-\rho}.
\]
This proves (5). If the two lower values coincide, only the upper formula remains and gives (6). If the two upper values coincide, only the lower formula remains and gives (7). The formulas agree at every knot. Since a cutting line has planar area zero, all closed-endpoint conventions give the same cap area.

On slice \(i\), write \(w=\lambda_i u\) with \(u\in\Delta\). Since
\(L(z)=\lambda_1m\), inequality (1) becomes
\[
L(u)\le
\frac{\lambda_1m+\sigma(1-i)}{\lambda_i}=t_i.
\]
The slice mass is therefore
\(D\lambda_i^2\Phi_{\gamma,\rho}(t_i)\), proving (8)-(9). The two horizontal halfspaces through the middle slice have masses
\(D(\lambda_0^2+\lambda_1^2)\) and
\(D(\lambda_1^2+\lambda_2^2)\), so (10) follows from
`400272f6de6c67bb`.

For the bottom slice, a spline branch changes exactly when \(t_0=b_k\), which is equivalent to \(\sigma=B_{0,k}\). For the top slice, it changes exactly when \(t_2=b_k\), which is equivalent to \(\sigma=B_{2,k}\). This proves that (11) is the complete finite breakpoint list. As \(\sigma\) tends to \(-\infty\), the bottom cap is empty and the top cap is full; as \(\sigma\) tends to \(+\infty\), the bottom cap is full and the top cap is empty. The splines are constant outside their extreme knots, so these tail values are attained for finite \(\sigma\), proving (12)-(13).

Between consecutive values in (11), the bottom and top spline branches are fixed. Each is constant or quadratic in its affine threshold, hence \(M_\pi\) is quadratic in \(\sigma\). A nonconstant quadratic attains its minimum on the interval closure at an endpoint or at its unique interior stationary point. Differentiating gives (14). If the derivative vanishes identically, the mass is constant on that interval and its value is already represented by either endpoint. Thus, for fixed \((\pi,\rho,\beta)\), the complete slope list is: the two tails (12)-(13), the six breakpoints (11), and feasible solutions of (14).

For \(0<\rho<1\), assign independently to \(t_0,m,t_2\) one of the four branches in (5). Together with the six permutations this gives at most
\(6\cdot4^3=384\) branch cells. Each cell is defined by linear inequalities comparing \(t_0,m,t_2\) with
\(\gamma,\gamma+\rho,\gamma+1\). On a cell, \(M_\pi\) is rational with denominator dividing \(\rho(1-\rho)\), and (14) is linear in \(\sigma\).

After substituting either a solution of (14) or a breakpoint from (11), the remaining \(\rho\)-minimum on each cell closure occurs in one of the following finite regimes:

1. \(\rho=0\) or \(\rho=1\), evaluated with (6) or (7);

2. \(m=b_k\), where the middle spline changes branch;

3. \(B_{i,k}=B_{j,\ell}\), where the ordering of slope breakpoints changes;

4. an interior stationary point obtained by differentiating the substituted rational candidate with respect to \(\rho\);

5. a stationary point along a breakpoint boundary, obtained by differentiating \(M_\pi(\beta,\rho,B_{i,k}(\rho))\) with respect to \(\rho\);

6. an intersection of two or more of the preceding boundary equations.

The branch inequalities are retained in every system. On \(0<\rho<1\), multiplying equations and weak inequalities only by suitable powers of the positive quantities \(\rho\) and \(1-\rho\) clears every denominator without changing feasibility. Cases \(\rho=0,1\) are evaluated separately by (6)-(7). Hence every candidate regime is described by a polynomial system, the number of systems is finite, and their coefficients are rational or real algebraic whenever the input data are. Compactness of every bounded cell closure, constancy on the two slope tails, and the explicit inclusion of every cell boundary prove that these systems contain the exact global minimizer.
statement:
Let \(\Delta\) be a nondegenerate triangle of area \(D\), let \(v_0\) be one of its vertices, and let
\[
A_i=v_0+\lambda_i(\Delta-v_0),\qquad \lambda_i>0,\quad i=0,1,2.
\]
After an invertible affine change of planar coordinates fixing \(v_0\), write
\(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,e_2\}\). For barycentric coordinates
\(\beta_j\ge0\), \(\beta_0+\beta_1+\beta_2=1\), put
\[
z=\lambda_1(\beta_1e_1+\beta_2e_2)\in A_1.
\]

Every nonhorizontal halfspace whose boundary contains \((1,z)\) has the form
\[
H(L,\sigma)=
\{(x,w):L(w-z)\le \sigma(1-x)\},
\tag{1}
\]
where \(L\ne0\) is linear and \(\sigma\in\mathbb R\). Positive rescaling of \((L,\sigma)\) changes neither the halfspace nor its mass. Put
\[
c_j=L(v_j),\qquad c_0=0,
\]
and normalize
\[
\max_jc_j-\min_jc_j=1.
\tag{2}
\]

Choose a permutation \(\pi=(\pi_0,\pi_1,\pi_2)\) satisfying
\(c_{\pi_0}\le c_{\pi_1}\le c_{\pi_2}\). There is a unique
\(\rho\in[0,1]\) such that
\[
c_{\pi_0}=\gamma,\qquad
c_{\pi_1}=\gamma+\rho,\qquad
c_{\pi_2}=\gamma+1,
\tag{3}
\]
where
\[
\gamma=
\begin{cases}
0,&\pi_0=0,\\
-\rho,&\pi_1=0,\\
-1,&\pi_2=0.
\end{cases}
\tag{4}
\]
Conversely, every permutation, every \(\rho\in[0,1]\), and (3)-(4) define a normalized nonzero \(L\).

Define
\[
\Phi_{\gamma,\rho}(t)
=
\frac{\operatorname{area}\{u\in\Delta:L(u)\le t\}}{D}.
\]
For \(0<\rho<1\),
\[
\Phi_{\gamma,\rho}(t)=
\begin{cases}
0,&t\le\gamma,\\
\dfrac{(t-\gamma)^2}{\rho},
&\gamma\le t\le\gamma+\rho,\\
1-\dfrac{(\gamma+1-t)^2}{1-\rho},
&\gamma+\rho\le t\le\gamma+1,\\
1,&t\ge\gamma+1.
\end{cases}
\tag{5}
\]
The exact tied-endpoint splines are
\[
\Phi_{\gamma,0}(t)=
\begin{cases}
0,&t\le\gamma,\\
1-(\gamma+1-t)^2,&\gamma\le t\le\gamma+1,\\
1,&t\ge\gamma+1,
\end{cases}
\tag{6}
\]
and
\[
\Phi_{\gamma,1}(t)=
\begin{cases}
0,&t\le\gamma,\\
(t-\gamma)^2,&\gamma\le t\le\gamma+1,\\
1,&t\ge\gamma+1.
\end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]

Put
\[
m=\sum_{j=0}^2\beta_jc_j,
\qquad
t_i=\frac{\lambda_1m+\sigma(1-i)}{\lambda_i}.
\tag{8}
\]
Then
\[
\frac{\mathcal H_2(S\cap H(L,\sigma))}{D}
=
M_\pi(\beta,\rho,\sigma)
:=
\sum_{i=0}^2\lambda_i^2
\Phi_{\gamma,\rho}(t_i).
\tag{9}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{h_S(1,z)}D
=
\min\left\{
\lambda_0^2+\lambda_1^2,\
\lambda_1^2+\lambda_2^2,\
\inf_{\substack{\pi\in\mathfrak S_3\\
\rho\in[0,1],\ \sigma\in\mathbb R}}
M_\pi(\beta,\rho,\sigma)
\right\}.
\tag{10}
\]

For fixed \((\pi,\rho,\beta)\), let
\[
(b_0,b_1,b_2)=(\gamma,\gamma+\rho,\gamma+1).
\]
All finite slope breakpoints are
\[
B_{0,k}=\lambda_0b_k-\lambda_1m,\qquad
B_{2,k}=\lambda_1m-\lambda_2b_k,
\qquad k=0,1,2.
\tag{11}
\]
The two unbounded endpoint values are
\[
M_\pi(\beta,\rho,-\infty)
=
\lambda_1^2\Phi_{\gamma,\rho}(m)+\lambda_2^2,
\tag{12}
\]
and
\[
M_\pi(\beta,\rho,+\infty)
=
\lambda_0^2+\lambda_1^2\Phi_{\gamma,\rho}(m).
\tag{13}
\]
Both values are attained on sufficiently far finite slope rays. On every open interval determined by the six breakpoints in (11), an interior slope minimizer satisfies
\[
\lambda_0\Phi'_{\gamma,\rho}(t_0)
=
\lambda_2\Phi'_{\gamma,\rho}(t_2).
\tag{14}
\]

For fixed algebraic \(\lambda_i\) and algebraic barycentric coordinates \(\beta_j\), equations (3)-(14), together with their stated branch inequalities, reduce the exact infimum in (10) to finitely many real-algebraic polynomial systems.
